title: SQL JOINs and Relationships
subtitle: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and relationships between tables.
description: Learn how multiple related tables can be combined to create powerful database queries.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand SQL JOINs and Relationships

Welcome to Lesson 6: SQL JOINs and Relationships. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “SQL JOINs and Relationships”. The goal is to iNNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and relationships between tables.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Joins combine rows from related tables using a relationship such as a customer ID. An INNER JOIN keeps matches, while a LEFT JOIN also retains rows from the left table that have no match.

blocks.title: Sample 1: SQL JOINs and Relationships in practice
blocks.code:
SELECT learners.display_name, courses.title
FROM enrollments
INNER JOIN learners ON learners.learner_id = enrollments.learner_id
INNER JOIN courses ON courses.course_id = enrollments.course_id;

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and relationships between tables. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A report must list every learner, even learners without a course enrollment. Which join preserves all learners?
options: A filter that removes unmatched rows.
blocks.explanation: A left join retains every row from the left-hand table even when no matching enrollment exists.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A left join retains every row from the left-hand table even when no matching enrollment exists.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A left join retains every row from the left-hand table even when no matching enrollment exists.

blocks.question: A join unexpectedly triples the output rows. What should be checked?
options: Whether the join keys uniquely identify the intended relationship and whether duplicate matches exist.
blocks.explanation: One-to-many relationships and incorrect join conditions can multiply rows.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. One-to-many relationships and incorrect join conditions can multiply rows.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. One-to-many relationships and incorrect join conditions can multiply rows.

blocks.text: Incorrect join conditions can multiply rows or drop records unexpectedly. Check primary-key and foreign-key relationships and compare row counts before and after joining.

blocks.title: Sample 3: SQL JOINs and Relationships in practice
blocks.code:
SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.learner_id) AS learners
FROM courses AS c
LEFT JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.course_id = c.course_id
GROUP BY c.course_id, c.title;

blocks.question: Two tables both have a column named id. How should the query avoid ambiguity?
options: Qualify the columns with table names or aliases.
Use SELECT * and hope the right one wins.
blocks.explanation: Qualified names show which table each column belongs to.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Qualified names show which table each column belongs to.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Qualified names show which table each column belongs to.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Use clear table aliases and qualify ambiguous column names. A join should express the actual relationship, not merely connect columns that happen to share a name.

blocks.title: Sample 4: SQL JOINs and Relationships in practice
blocks.code:
SELECT results.learner_id, learners.display_name, results.score
FROM lesson_results AS results
JOIN learners ON learners.learner_id = results.learner_id
WHERE results.score < 50;

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
